children: Rising bond yields, higher MCLR and a shift towards bank borrowings could put pressure on NBFC margins and returns, with the impact varying significantly across segments, says JM Financial

India’s non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) are facing renewed pressure on funding costs as market yields rise and expectations of a potential policy rate hike strengthen, with the impact likely to vary depending on their asset and liability structures, according to a thematic research report by JM Financial Institutional Securities.

The report said yields across government securities, treasury bills, corporate bonds and NBFC debt have risen by around 20-90 basis points since June 2026, while the one-year marginal cost of funds-based lending rate (MCLR) has increased by around 30 basis points since March 2026. At the same time, NBFCs have increased their reliance on bank borrowing, which typically reprices faster than fixed-rate instruments such as commercial paper (CP) and non-convertible debentures (NCDs).

JM Financial said the combination could result in a faster increase in the cost of funds for NBFCs if rates rise further. Its sensitivity analysis suggests that a 50-basis-point rate hike could have an impact of between -20 basis points and +10 basis points on return on assets (RoA), depending on the business and funding structure of individual lenders.
Bank Funding To NBFCs Accelerates

Bank lending to NBFCs and housing finance companies (HFCs) has accelerated sharply after slowing in FY25. According to the report, bank loans to NBFCs/HFCs grew around 27 per cent year-on-year in FY26 and accelerated further to 32 per cent in Q1FY27, reaching approximately ₹21.1 trillion by June 2026.

The share of NBFC/HFC loans in total bank credit also recovered to around 9.7 per cent in Q1FY27 from 9 per cent in FY25. More significantly, NBFCs accounted for around 15 per cent of incremental bank credit in Q1FY27, compared with only around 5 per cent in FY25.

The shift has been particularly pronounced among private banks. Private-bank lending to NBFCs contracted by 9 per cent in FY25 before rebounding to 27 per cent in FY26 and 34 per cent in Q1FY27. Public sector banks continued to hold the largest share of NBFC credit, at around 68 per cent at the end of Q1FY27.
Shift Away From NCDs
The stronger reliance on bank funding has come alongside a moderation in alternative sources of finance, particularly NCDs.

The report said NCD issuance growth turned negative from Q2FY26 and remained weak through Q1FY27, when issuance declined 37 per cent year-on-year. Outstanding NCD growth also moderated from 15 per cent in Q1FY26 to 8 per cent in Q1FY27.
Commercial paper issuance, meanwhile, grew around 18 per cent year-on-year in Q1FY27, with outstanding CP rising around 8 per cent to approximately Rs 5.4 trillion.

JM Financial noted that bank loans linked to the repo rate, external benchmarks or MCLR generally reprice faster, while CP and NCDs tend to remain fixed until their respective rollover or maturity. CP typically has a tenor of around three to 12 months, while NCDs generally have a three-to-five-year tenor.

As a result, the increasing share of bank loans in NBFC liabilities means any rate increase could pass through to funding costs faster than it would have when a larger proportion of liabilities were held in fixed-rate instruments.
Rate Cuts Had Lowered Funding Costs

NBFCs had benefited significantly from the previous rate-cut cycle. The Reserve Bank of India cut the repo rate by a cumulative 125 basis points between February and October 2025, taking it from 6.50 per cent to 5.25 per cent. The repo rate remained at 5.25 per cent through the August 2026 policy review.

JM Financial calculated that the cost of funds for its NBFC coverage universe declined by around 80 basis points between Q3FY25 and Q4FY26, representing roughly 62 per cent pass-through of the 125-basis-point repo rate reduction.
However, the benefit appears to have peaked. Nineteen of the 23 companies covered by JM Financial saw their cost of funds increase between Q4FY26 and Q1FY27, by around 10 basis points on average.

The increase was led by Fusion Finance, L&T Finance, CreditAccess Grameen and Aditya Birla Capital. The rise coincided with an increase in the one-year MCLR from 8.4 per cent in Q4FY26 to 8.7 per cent in August 2026, alongside higher corporate and NBFC bond yields.
Market Already Pricing In Rate Hike Risk

The report noted that the bond market appears to be pricing in some possibility of a further increase in policy rates. The spread between the 10-year government security yield and the repo rate was around 180 basis points in September 2026, compared with a long-term average of approximately 130 basis points.

Based on this gap, JM Financial said the market could be factoring in around 50 basis points of repo-rate increases in the near term. The spread between five-year NBFC AAA yields and the repo rate had also widened to around 300 basis points, compared with a long-term average of around 190 basis points.

The report said yields across several funding benchmarks had risen substantially since June. For example, the 12-month Treasury bill yield was 5.9 per cent in September, while the 10-year government security yield stood at 5.9 per cent. Five-year NBFC AAA yields were around 7.9 per cent.
Asset Mix To Determine Impact
The effect of higher rates will not be uniform across NBFCs, with the composition of loan books playing a key role.

JM Financial said housing finance companies generally have a high proportion of floating-rate loans, with several HFCs having around 70-100 per cent of their loan books linked to floating rates. This could allow them to reprice assets as funding costs rise.

By contrast, vehicle financiers, microfinance institutions (MFIs), MSME lenders and gold financiers have a much higher proportion of fixed-rate loans. The report estimates that around 60-100 per cent of loan books in these segments are fixed-rate, limiting their ability to immediately reprice loans when funding costs increase.

Among diversified NBFCs, the picture is mixed. Aditya Birla Capital, Piramal Finance and Tata Capital have relatively high floating-rate loan exposure, while L&T Finance, HDB Financial Services and Poonawalla Fincorp have a larger share of fixed-rate loans.
Housing Financiers Better Positioned

The report's sensitivity analysis indicates that housing financiers could see a comparatively favourable impact from a rate hike because of the higher floating-rate component of their loan books and comparatively slower repricing of some liabilities.
JM Financial said prime HFCs such as LIC Housing Finance, PNB Housing Finance and Bajaj Housing Finance appear positioned to benefit in terms of the potential impact on FY28 estimated NIMs and RoAs.

Vehicle financiers, meanwhile, are expected to face a negative impact on NIMs and RoAs. MFIs and several MSME lenders could also face pressure because of the mismatch between fixed-rate lending and their funding structures.
Within diversified NBFCs, the impact is expected to remain company-specific, depending on the balance between fixed and floating-rate assets and liabilities.
Shift To Bank Loans Increases Repricing Exposure

At the company level, the shift towards bank funding has been broad-based. Between FY25 and Q1FY27, the bank-loan share increased sharply for several lenders, including SBFC Finance, Poonawalla Fincorp, LIC Housing Finance, HDB Financial Services and L&T Finance.
For example, SBFC's bank-loan share increased from 53 per cent to 62 per cent, while HDB's rose from 37 per cent to 46 per cent. L&T Finance's share increased from 56 per cent to 62 per cent.

In most cases, the increase in bank funding came at the expense of NCDs. JM Financial said this suggests that several NBFCs substituted fixed-rate, longer-duration NCDs with floating-rate bank loans during the rate-cut cycle to capture lower borrowing costs more quickly.

A smaller group moved in the opposite direction. Poonawalla Fincorp reduced its bank-loan share from 70 per cent in FY25 to 58 per cent in Q1FY27, while its NCD share increased from 6 per cent to 31 per cent. Aditya Birla Capital also reduced its reliance on bank loans while increasing its NCD exposure.
The report said this strategy of locking in longer-duration fixed-rate funding while rates were low could provide greater insulation as yields rise.
Refinancing Risk To Rise In FY27-28
The rising cost environment could become more relevant as a significant portion of NBFC NCDs comes up for repricing or refinancing over the next two financial years.

JM Financial estimates that NCDs account for around 2-48 per cent of borrowings across its coverage universe, while maturing NCDs during the remainder of FY27 and FY28 account for around 10-60 per cent of existing NCDs for different lenders.
Several large NBFCs face meaningful repricing gaps, although recent credit-rating upgrades could provide some companies with access to cheaper refinancing.

The report also noted that bank borrowings account for around 20-75 per cent of borrowings for most covered NBFCs. T-bill-linked bank borrowing could reprice immediately as market yields rise, while the impact of higher MCLR is expected to emerge with a lag in the second half of FY27 and FY28.
Impact On Margins To Vary Across NBFCs

Overall, JM Financial expects a potential 50-basis-point rate hike to have a -20-basis-point to +10-basis-point impact on NBFC/HFC RoAs, with an estimated -8 per cent to +7 per cent impact on earnings per share, all else being equal.
The report stressed that the impact depends not only on the liability structure but also on the composition of each lender's loan book, as well as growth and asset-quality trends.

It said housing financiers appear better positioned for a rate increase, while vehicle financiers, MFIs and gold financiers face greater sensitivity. Diversified and MSME-focused lenders are likely to see a more mixed, company-specific impact.

JM Financial also noted that its assessment of companies is not based solely on net interest margin dynamics. Loan growth remains an important factor in its analysis, particularly as asset quality across the sector remains relatively benign, according to the report.
